proof.text: An elementary contraction $h:P\to Q$ is an epimorphism on morphisms of $k$-schemes. Indeed, if $a,b:Q\to Z$ have $ah=bh$, their restrictions to the other pushout vertex $\operatorname{Spec}k$ agree: precompose with the $k$-point $[1:0]\in A\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$ (the ring map $k[t]\to k$, $t\mapsto0$, in the standard affine chart). The pushout universal property now gives $a=b$. For pointed morphisms the marking maps agree too, since the contraction's marking map is an isomorphism. Composites and isomorphisms preserve this cancellation property. The same pushout universal property gives a unique isomorphism over $P$ between two elementary contractions of the same component.

source.place: Appendix B, p. 58, elementary pushout paragraph; its universal property

proof.text: By [lem-trf-exceptional-contraction-diamond], the noncollapse hypothesis persists after each elementary contraction. Isomorphisms also preserve it, as well as semistability, marking, and exceptionality. We prove the following strengthened claim by strong induction on $n$: if $\pi:P\to S$ is a sequence of exactly $n$ elementary contractions and a final isomorphism, and the induced reference map on $S$ has no exceptional component, then every single elementary contraction $h:P\to Q$ admits a factorization $\pi=v h$ in which $v:Q\to S$ is a sequence of exactly $n-1$ elementary contractions and a final isomorphism. The assertion for $n=0$ means that no such $h$ exists. Isomorphisms between intermediate representatives can be absorbed by conjugating the next pushout; this uses only the pushout universal property, not an identification of topological quotients with scheme quotients.

source.place: Appendix B, Lemma B.3, p. 58; explicit length induction for elementary contractions

proof.text: For $n=0$, $P$ is isomorphic to $S$ over $C$, so it has no exceptional component and no elementary contraction can start. For $n>0$, write $\pi=\pi_Ah_A$, where $h_A$ contracts $A$ and $\pi_A$ has length $n-1$. Let $h_B:P\to P_B$ be the arbitrary single contraction. If $B=A$, the pushout isomorphism $e:P_B\simeq P_A$ from Step 1 satisfies $e h_B=h_A$, and $v=\pi_Ae$ is the required remaining sequence of length $n-1$.

source.place: Appendix B, B.3, p. 58; base case and identical first contractions

proof.text: Suppose $B\ne A$. Apply [lem-trf-exceptional-contraction-diamond] to the two supplied first contractions: it gives elementary maps $j_A:P_A\to T$ and $j_B:P_B\to T$ with $j_Ah_A=j_Bh_B$. The induction claim at length $n-1$, applied to $\pi_A$ and $j_A$, gives $\pi_A=w j_A$, where $w:T\to S$ has length $n-2$. If $n=1$ this situation is impossible, since $P_A$ would already have no exceptional component but $j_A$ contracts one. Thus in the distinct-component case $n\ge2$, and $v=w j_B$ has length $n-1$, with $v h_B=w j_Bh_B=w j_Ah_A=\pi_Ah_A=\pi$. The hypotheses for the induction on $P_A$ are exactly its semistability, induced reference map and noncollapse property supplied by the diamond lemma; the terminal map on $S$ is unchanged. This proves the strengthened single-step claim.

source.place: Appendix B, B.3, p. 58; order independence, with the local diamond made explicit

proof.text: Write the arbitrary partial sequence as $q=e h_m\cdots h_1$, with final isomorphism $e:Q_m\simeq P'$. Starting with $v_0=\pi$, apply the single-step claim successively to $v_{i-1}:Q_{i-1}\to S$ and $h_i:Q_{i-1}\to Q_i$. It gives $v_i:Q_i\to S$ with $v_{i-1}=v_i h_i$ and length $n-i$. All hypotheses persist by Step 2, and $S=P^{\mathrm{st}}$ remains terminal throughout. If $i>n$ were possible, the next $h_i$ would start at the length-zero, already terminal source, contradicting the base case; hence $m\le n$. The map $u=v_m e^{-1}$ is a pointed $k$-morphism and satisfies $u q=\pi$. For $m=0$ this reads $u=\pi e^{-1}$ and covers an arbitrary final isomorphism.

source.place: Appendix B, B.3, p. 58, final factorization assertion; iteration of the proved single-step claim

proof.text: If $u_1q=u_2q$, Step 1 cancels the composite $q$ and gives $u_1=u_2$. If $\pi':P\to S'$ is another terminal sequence, the factorization just proved in each direction gives $a:S'\to S$ and $b:S\to S'$ with $a\pi'=\pi$ and $b\pi=\pi'$. Then $ab\pi=\pi$ and $ba\pi'=\pi'$, so cancellation gives $ab=1_S$ and $ba=1_{S'}$. This is the unique isomorphism compatible with the maps from $P$. Empty markings and a zero-length sequence cause no change in these arguments, and connectedness or properness over $k$ was never used.

source.place: Appendix B, Lemma B.3, p. 58, uniqueness up to unique isomorphism

title: Stable blowdown quotient and its factorization through partial exceptional contractions
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], let $(P,M)$ be a semistable multipointed $k$-curve [def-trf-multipointed-curve, def-trf-multipointed-curve-modification], and let $r:P\to C$ be a morphism to a $k$-scheme [def-pc-scheme]. Assume that the image under $r$ of every connected component of $P$ contains more than one point; thus no whole connected component is collapsed by the reference map. An $r$-exceptional component is an irreducible component $A\simeq\mathbf P^1_k$ [def-sc-p1-standard] with singleton image in $C$ and at most two distinct points in $A\cap(M\cup P_{\mathrm{sing}})$. An elementary $r$-exceptional contraction means the scheme pushout of $P\leftarrow A\to\operatorname{Spec}k$, with semistable pointed quotient and marking transported isomorphically; the map to $C$ factors through that quotient. For later contractions use the induced map to $C$ and the marking and singular points of the current quotient. Suppose a finite sequence of elementary $r$-exceptional contractions, followed by an isomorphism, gives $\pi:(P,M)\to(P^{\mathrm{st}},M^{\mathrm{st}})$ whose target has no exceptional component for its induced map to $C$. Then for every finite sequence $q:(P,M)\to(P',M')$ of elementary $r$-exceptional contractions, also allowing a final isomorphism, there is a unique morphism of pointed $k$-curves $u:(P',M')\to(P^{\mathrm{st}},M^{\mathrm{st}})$ such that $\pi=u\circ q$. In particular the terminal quotient is unique up to unique isomorphism compatible with $\pi$. Connectedness and properness over $k$ are not assumed; the noncollapse hypothesis on $r$ is required; the assertion applies component by component, and the existence of $\pi$ as a quotient which is still a curve is part of the hypothesis.
